It was far, far harder to copy and distribute and manufacture inventions back then, than it is today.

It just wasn't anywhere near as economically or logistically feasible for someone to see something da Vinci invented, and then go off and build market distribute and profit from it themselves.

Plans had to be physically transferred or manually copied (limiting access), everything had to be hand crafted (limiting profit margin and distribution potential), and the logistics of global transport meant that unless somebody was geographically near somebody else, they were unlikely to ever compete for the same customers.

After the advent of digital data, interchangeable parts, globalization of trade, and mass production, things that were not possible back then and so did not need any protections against, are now possible.

I note that not everybody has da Vinci's intrinsic drive to create and invent. I believe the concept behind patents is to provide a known path to monetization of an invention, to encourage (one could even say enshrine) the act of inventing in a society with an economic policy rooted in capitalism.
Back then they used the patron model where someone gave you money up front for you to live on so you didn't have to care about making money from your invention.

So intersting note about Da Vinci specifically. He actually did patent all his inventions. There are quite a few theories that he didn't really invent most of his inventions, so much as was the first to patent them. The first "Patent Law" the world ever saw was enacted in Venice in 1474 Source. However Florence had been awarding patents since as early as 1421 Source, to a man generally considered to be one of the key members of the Renaissance, Fillipo Brunelleschi Source.

There is even some anecdotal evidence from as far back as 500 BC to suggest ancient Greek states had patent laws, guaranteeing monopolies to inventors for a period of one year Source.

Anyways, there is SOME place for patents. However the way patents are currently being used is a bastardization of what they were originaly intended to do. It was meant to protect an intelligent inventor from having his idea stolen by someone who had more capital. Or to at least give him a reasonable window of time to make some profit for himself. I think the real problem also has a lot to do with corporations being legal persons, which first allowed patent law to be interpreted in a rather nebulous way. What does "until death" mean to a corporate entity?
Also, there's no patents at all in Math, Physics, or any other science field other than computer science. And yet - innovation still works there.

That's all well and all, but you can patent EXISTING DNA sequences - even though that's actually discoveries.
